display_title: Official Review of Submission4000 by Reviewer 3VJ2

summary.value: The authors propose a method for uncertainty quantification based on Bayesian inference that can be used with existing MLIP architectures. They evaluate the method on synthetic data, NH3, and a silica glass system. They evaluate UQ performance and accuracy on energy and force metrics.

strengths.value:
- Uncertainty quantification is an important aspect not yet fully addressed by the MLIP community. 
- The proposed method is motivated well and grounded in existing work.
- In general, I agree with the authors that tackling UQ / generalization with MLIPs is an important area, especially since many important scientific applications deal explicitly with extrapolation.

weaknesses.value:
While I think the method makes sense and is well presented, the evaluation makes it hard to justify the benefit of the proposed approach:
- The models considered are not the best models. Although the authors mention that the method is not currently amenable to new models like UMA, if the authors are claiming to evaluate generalization capability, then it is important to consider models explicitly trained with broad coverage. While the authors look at Orb, it is hard to evaluate how meaningful any E/F improvements are. The difference seems to go away as data increases and the relative performance benefit it quite small compared to the difference between the PaiNN model trained from scratch and the pre-trained Orb. The UQ performance seems to be worse here than an ensemble.
- In such data-limited regimes, it feels like a deep learning model is not the best choice. A simpler model like sGDML [1] often performs quite well with limited data. How does sGDML perform in terms of UQ and errors?     
- The authors only evaluate F/E regression metrics without evaluating downstream performance (like MD simulations).
- It would strengthen the paper to more clearly address the computational costs during both training and inference. The authors claim multiple times that these models are cheaper than ensembles but don't explicitly quantify the differences. If the cost of having multiple models is an issue, then different readout heads could be evaluated as an alternative. In addition, there are many other cheap ways of evaluating uncertainty, including training a smaller ML model [1]. Bayesian neural networks are also known to be hard to train at scale so it is hard to evaluate how generally applicable this method would be (or if the authors envision this as just a fine-tuning strategy).
- There are a number of existing works that discuss out-of-distribution performance and benchmarks for MLIPs and might be relevant for this work [2,3,4].  


[1] Chmiela, S., Sauceda, H., Poltavsky, I., Müller, K.R., & Tkatchenko, A. (2019). sGDML: Constructing accurate and data efficient molecular force fields using machine learning. Computer Physics Communications, 240, 38–45.

[2] Bowen Deng, Yunyeong Choi, Peichen Zhong, Janosh Riebesell, Shashwat Anand, Zhuohan Li, KyuJung Jun, Kristin A. Persson, & Gerbrand Ceder. (2024). Overcoming systematic softening in universal machine learning interatomic potentials by fine-tuning.

[3] Tobias Kreiman, & Aditi S. Krishnapriyan. (2025). Understanding and Mitigating Distribution Shifts For Machine Learning Force Fields.

[4] Chanussot, L., Das, A., Goyal, S., Lavril, T., Shuaibi, M., Riviere, M., Tran, K., Heras-Domingo, J., Ho, C., Hu, W., Palizhati, A., Sriram, A., Wood, B., Yoon, J., Parikh, D., Zitnick, C., & Ulissi, Z. (2021). Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) Dataset and Community Challenges. ACS Catalysis, 11(10), 6059–6072.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent evaluating our paper. We appreciate that the reviewer recognizes our work as addressing “*an important aspect not yet fully addressed by the MLIP community*” and finds our method “*well motivated and grounded in existing work*.” Below we answer the concerns raised by the reviewer in **weakness** in the hope of further strengthening the paper.

> The models considered are not the best models... if the authors are claiming to evaluate generalization capability...

We thank the reviewer for raising the concern regarding the utility of our approach in light of recent advances in the field. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to present a **scalable and efficient method** for both prediction and uncertainty estimation in GNNs and MLIPs that requires only a single model training, achieving performance comparable to or exceeding standard ensembling approaches. **We do not claim generalizability anywhere in the paper**, but we demonstrate that our method provides reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) when trained from scratch (Experiments 1 and 2) or when fine-tuning a pretrained universal MLIP (Experiment 3).

> While the authors look at Orb, it is hard to evaluate how meaningful any E/F improvements are.... The UQ performance seems to be worse here than an ensemble.

In the ORB experiments, we show that we can **effectively fine-tune a pretrained Universal MLIP (ORBv3 OMAT24) using BLIP**, achieving a **~7% improvement in force error** compared to standard MLIP fine-tuning, and a **~10% improvement** compared to the pretrained network in the low-data regime. This is particularly valuable given the high cost of generating labeled data. Furthermore, our method **does not degrade prediction accuracy as the dataset size increases**, suggesting promising potential for scaling to larger datasets. 
Finally, our approach in the ORB experiment achieves a **substantial improvement in calibration** over Deep Ensemble Fine-Tuning (0.032 vs. 0.247). We would be grateful for clarification regarding the comment that “UQ performance seems to be worse here than an ensemble,” as our results suggest improved performance.

> In such data-limited regimes, it feels like a deep learning model...

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. While we find the methodology very interesting, our primary focus in this work is to benchmark graph-based machine learning models, as our approach does not currently extend to other model types. We agree that, in low-data regimes, graph-based MLIPs may underperform simpler models. However, the Ammonia experiment was specifically chosen to **stress-test our method in a heavily out-of-distribution (OOD) low-data regime**, which is a common challenge for MLIPs, and we compared against the models already presented in literature [1]

> The authors only evaluate F/E regression metrics without evaluating downstream performance (like MD simulations).

We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion! We have added a downstream task in which uncertainties are used in an active learning loop to refine UMLIP. Specifically, we used the recently published MatPES [1] dataset (400K selected molecular structures) to fine-tune ORBv3 using active learning: uncertainties are used to identify the structures for which the model is most uncertain, which are then labeled with reference DFT computations and used for further fine-tuning. This cycle is repeated multiple times. 
The results show that BLIP with uncertainty-driven fine-tuning outperforms standard fine-tuning, in which molecules are selected at random, demonstrating that uncertainties obtained with BLIP can be effectively leveraged in an active learning loop (see section 4.4 for full results). MD experiment might also be another interesting application, but we leave it for future works.


> It would strengthen the paper to more clearly address the computational costs during both training and inference...

We thank the reviewer for the great suggestion. We have added a detailed discussion on parameter counts and FLOPs in Appendix E, comparing to Deep Ensemble.

Approaches such as multi-head readouts or small auxiliary models have comparable overhead in FLOPs but generally produce weaker epistemic uncertainty estimates (see Table 2 as example), as they do not model the latent variability of the backbone. Multi-head readouts in particular share all backbone parameters, limiting the diversity required for reliable uncertainty quantification. 

> There are a number of existing works that discuss out-of-distribution performance and benchmarks for MLIPs and might be relevant for this work [2,3,4].

Thank you, we have added those references in related work!

[1] Tan, Aik Rui, et al. "Single-model uncertainty quantification in neural network potentials does not consistently outperform model ensembles." npj Computational Materials 9.1 (2023): 225.

summary.value: The paper describes how a particular formulation of variational inference can be applied to the setting of a machine learning interatomic potential. The method uses local reparametrization and involves input dependent variance scaling factors: the variance of each weight is specified as the squared mean value multiplied by an input dependent scale (adaptive variance term). It is discussed how the method retains equivariance (in distribution) when used with an equivariant GNN architecture. The method is demonstrated on a simple N-body system, a small ammonia dataset with training data near equilibrium an out of equilibrium test data, and finetuning a pretrained ORB model on a SiO2 dataset. The results show favorable peformance in comparison with deep ensembles.

strengths.value:
The paper is well written and easy to follow.

The proposed modeling approach is reasonable and seems to work well. It is very general and can be applied to a long range of problems, also outside MLIPs.

weaknesses.value:
Deep ensembles are commonly used for UQ in MLIPs, and there are several papers that focus on different ways to do this, however this literature is not cited sufficiently. In particular it would be beneficial with a discussion on how posthoc calibration is beneficial. 

All examples are in the small data regime and for the most part concerned with out of distribution uncertainty. Typically this means high sensitivity to hyperparameter choices. Often a slightly over-regularized model can trade in distribution performance for better out-of-distribution performance. However, in-distribution performance is not reported, and it is not described in sufficient detail how baselines including deep ensembles were tuned. 

The paper is positioned (and titled) as a Bayesian method, however when using a data dependent approximate posterior, the Bayesian interpretation is a stretch.

The discussion around equivariance and invariance in distribution in section 3.3 is very interesting and important in my opinion. I would have liked to see this extended to a more formal analysis, showing exactly when and how invariant coefficients (alpha and beta) is enough to guarantee equivariance in distribution for an equivariant base architecture. Furthermore, the argument that this does not hold for architectures based on irreducible representations of SO(3) would be very interesting to unfold more.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent evaluating our paper. We appreciate the reviewer finds our method "*very general and can be applied to a long range of problems, also outside MLIPs*", and we also appreciate the reviewer finds our paper "*is well written and easy to follow*". Below we address the raised points in **weakness** in the hope to clarify and further improve the paper.

> Deep ensembles are commonly used for UQ in MLIPs, and ...

We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In the initial submission, the page limit constrained the length of our related work section; however, we have now added a dedicated paragraph addressing this point. The new paragraph, along with the additional reference, is highlighted in blue in Section 2.4. We would be happy to consider any further improvements the reviewer might suggest.

> All examples are in the small data regime and for the most part concerned with ...

We thank the reviewer for the comment, and we address reviewer concers below for each experiment. 

Regarding the **low data regime**, we agree with the reviewer that the ammonia experiment is a low data regime (only 78 geomtries in the training dataset). This experiments was appositaly chosen to **stress-test our method on heavily out-of-distribution (OOD) low data regime**, which is a common scenario in simulation based chemistry (the chemical space is vast and DFT labelled data are expensive). Unfortunately, we do not have labelled test data in-distribution, therefore we did not report that metric in the paper. To show that it is a fair evaluation we report here the validation error (averaged over 4 seeds) for in distribution data for the ammonia (notice that [1] does not report errors for the validation dataset, thus we can not directly compare).

**Ammonia Experiment Validation Dataset**

| Model   | MAE Energy (kcal/mol) | MAE Forces  (kcal/mol/Å) |
|:-------:|:---------------------:|:------------------------:|
| BLIP| $0.28$ | $2.02$  |


The results report a clear degradation of model accuracy when OOD data are tested (Table 2 main paper), which is expected, compared to the Validation dataset. The validation ECE for forces (0.095 ± 0.008) is in accordance with the OOD calibration reported in the paper (Table 3), showing that the method can mantain the same level of calibration for OOD data.

Finally, for the no low-data regime, we have added an experiment addressing this issue. We use the very recent published MatPES [1] dataset (400K selected molecular structures) in an active learning loop for finetuing ORBv3, where uncertainties are used to improve the pretrained model by selecting the structures for which the model is most uncertain. After these structures are selected, reference DFT computations are performed, and the model is further fine-tuned. We repeat multiple time this cycle. The results show that BLIP with uncertainty-driven fine-tuning outperforms standard fine-tuning, in which molecules are selected at random, showing that uncertainties with BLIP can be used in an active learning loop. Full results in section 4.4


> The paper is positioned (and titled) as a Bayesian method ...

We thank the reviewer for the comment and are happy to clarify our statement. Our approach is an amortized variational inference method in which the amortization is performed over molecular graph structures. While amortized VI indeed uses *data-dependent* approximate posteriors, this does not preclude a Bayesian interpretation. Many established bayesian deep learning [2, 3, 4] methods adopt the same paradigm: a parametric inference network is trained to approximate the true posterior, yielding a data-dependent approximate posterior distribution optimized jointly with the generative model. 

> The discussion around equivariance and invariance in distribution in section 3.3 is very interesting ...

Thank you for finding this point interesting, and for the constructive feedback. We are happy to elaborate further, and we have added an Appendix section (see Section A.3), where we formally prove that the BLIP update rule in Equation 7 preserves the equivariance of the MLIP model (this also applies to UMA and MACE architectures). We then explain why, if instead of sampling the weights one samples the activations (local reparameterization), equivariance is broken for models that use linear transformations across irreps dimensions. We hope this clarification strengthens the argument and helps future readers extend the methodology. Thank you again for the insightful suggestion!

Thank you for the very constructive questions, we are happy to respond to them below:

1. We added a reference of Figure 1, thank you for spotting it!

2. Thank you for raising this point. As normally done with amortized variational inference optimization [5] we do weight the KL term, even if we did not notice substantial improvement in the final accuracies. We have alsop highlited in the main text.

3. There is no a fundamental reason, we just found more intuitive to think about the sampling process rather than writing the full distirbution.

4. Exactly! We changed to the notation and rewrote everything in terms of distributions in order to avoid misunderstandings, thank you.

5. The baseline model results are directly taken from [5], while our MLIP network uses the same hyperparameters the authors in [5] used (to have a fair comparison), as reported in appendix C.2.

6. Thank you for the constructive feedback. Indeed different methods are available for finetuing. We did a full finetuing as suggested in the ORBv3 official repository [see here](https://github.com/orbital-materials/orb-models?tab=readme-ov-file#finetuning). Our scope is not apply BLIP to the most innovative finetuing startegies (this can be a nice futher work), but rather to show that BLIP can enhance finetuing with both better accuracy and the addition of uncertainties.

7. Thanks for the question that help us in improving the writing. The gaussian dropout assumes that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are greater than zero. A way to accoplish this is to predict a number $p\in[0,1]$ and then apply the transformation $\frac{p}{1-p}$, we have made this more clear in the main text.

8. For the hyperparameters $\lambda$ and $p$, we performed an initial hyperparameter search and selected the values that achieved the best validation accuracy (not UQ metrics). Specifically, we conducted a grid search over $\lambda \in \{0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0\}$ and $p \in \{0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8\}$. We did not observe substantial variation in validation accuracy across this range, which suggests that the method is reasonably robust to these choices. We also think that further works might suggest better priors and optimization startegies.

9. For all models and among all experiments, the validation dataset is used to select the best checkpoint, corresponding to the smallest validation loss. The validation loss is computed using the same loss function as in training, but evaluated on the validation set. We have added this in the main text at the beginning of section C.


[1] Tan, Aik Rui, et al. "Single-model uncertainty quantification in neural network potentials does not consistently outperform model ensembles." npj Computational Materials 9.1 (2023): 225.

[2] Kingma, Diederik P., and Max Welling. "Auto-encoding variational bayes." arXiv preprint arXiv:1312.6114 (2013).

[3] Rezende, Danilo Jimenez, Shakir Mohamed, and Daan Wierstra. "Stochastic backpropagation and approximate inference in deep generative models." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2014.

[4] Tomczak, Jakub M. "Deep Generative Modeling: From Probabilistic Framework to Generative AI." Entropy 27.3 (2025): 238.

[5] Higgins, Irina, et al. "beta-vae: Learning basic visual concepts with a constrained variational framework." International conference on learning representations. 2017.

comment.value:
**Reviews weakness**

>>Deep ensembles are commonly used for UQ in MLIPs, and ...

>We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In the initial submission, the page limit constrained the length of our related work section; however, we have now added a dedicated paragraph addressing this point. The new paragraph, along with the additional reference, is highlighted in blue in Section 2.4. We would be happy to consider any further improvements the reviewer might suggest.

I appreciate the added paragraph citing some of the relevant literature. However, I do think the phrasing regarding post-hoc calibration is fair. Approximate Bayesian method also do not come with calibration guarantees. Post-hoc methods such as conformal prediction can offer theoretical guarantees, provided one has access to an independent sample from the target distribution. In many settings this assumption is realistic, and these methods tend to perform very well in practice.

>>All examples are in the small data regime and for the most part concerned with ...

>...Unfortunately, we do not have labelled test data in-distribution, therefore we did not report that metric in the paper... 

I would very much have appreciated a direct comparison on in-distribution uncertainties, or other experiments that highlight the in/out distribution tradeoff.

>>The paper is positioned (and titled) as a Bayesian method ...

>...Our approach is an amortized variational inference method in which the amortization is performed over molecular graph structures. 

In deep generative models with latent variables assigned per data point, the posterior over these latents naturally depends on the data, which motivates the use of amortized inference. In contrast, for the MLIPs discussed here, the posterior is over global parameters and is therefore not data-dependent. I understand that the method you propose may perform well in practice, but I am unclear on its Bayesian interpretation

>>The discussion around equivariance and invariance in distribution in section 3.3 is very interesting ...

>...we have added an Appendix section (see Section A.3) ... if instead of sampling the weights one samples the activations (local reparameterization), equivariance is broken...

Thank you - this is much appreciated. However, I think the phrasing around local reparametrization for equivariant linear maps is a bit imprecise. A linear layer operating on an irrep would scale all components equally (weight sharing), and if we use the local reparametrization trick this will result in a non-diagonal covariance matrix. Thus, local reparametrization is possible but it just requires a slightly more involved sampling procedure. That said, this is not a critical point, as it does not affect the main contributions of the paper—I just found it an interesting nuance worth noting.

comment.value:
We sincerely appreciate your time and the constructive feedback on our submission. We have carefully addressed all of your comments and questions, and we hope our clarifications satisfactorily resolve the concerns you raised. Thank you again for your thoughtful review and we hope our response will lead to consider our work more favorably.

**Reviews weakness**

> I appreciate the added paragraph.....

We thank the reviewer for their comment and agree that conformal predictions are highly effective for post-hoc calibration, and that Bayesian methods do not come with formal calibration guarantees. Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript text from:

"For these reasons, we present a Bayesian approach that is scalable, requiring only a single trained model, and calibrated, offering a practical and efficient solution for UQ in MLIPs."

to:

"For these reasons, we present a Bayesian approach that is scalable, requiring only a single trained model, and **empirically exhibits good calibration**, offering a practical and efficient solution for UQ in MLIPs."

Regarding conformal prediction, while we have not explored it in this work, we believe it represents a valuable direction for future research.

> I would very much have appreciated a direct comparison on in-distribution uncertainties, or other experiments that highlight the in/out distribution tradeoff.

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In our first experiment (the Coulomb experiment), we explicitly evaluate in-distribution uncertainties. Additionally, we have included a new experiment (see Section 4.4) where in-distribution uncertainties are used to guide active learning fine-tuning, demonstrating clear improvements over standard fine-tuning.

> In deep generative models with...

We thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. We would like to clarify that our method does perform amortized inference, but the amortization occurs over individual atomic structures rather than over an entire dataset. In analogy with generative models, the latent variables in our setting correspond to the model weights, while each single atomic structure plays the role of an individual data point. Consequently, the inferred parameters are local to each structure, not global across the dataset.
We appreciate the opportunity to elaborate on this perspective and remain open to further discussion. If the reviewer believes this distinction should be emphasized more clearly in the main manuscript, we would be happy to include an explicit clarification.

> Thank you - this is much appreciated. However, I think the phrasing around local reparametrization ...

You are indeed right. However, sampling the covariance matrix would incur a computational cost that is essentially comparable to sampling the weights directly. This is precisely why we state that the local reparameterization trick is not applicable in our setting: the original purpose of the local reparameterization trick is to avoid such costly sampling procedures by pushing randomness to activations rather than weights. In that setting, performing local reparameterization would not provide any computational benefit, as it still requires sampling objects of similar complexity to the full weight matrix.

**Reviews questions**

> If the results are taken directly from [5], why not include ...

For the MAE on energies and forces, we used the results reported in Supplementary Figure 22 of the original publication (see [here](https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41524-023-01180-8/MediaObjects/41524_2023_1180_MOESM1_ESM.pdf#page=30.09)).
For the ECE, we report the values presented in the main text of the same work. The authors refer to this metric as Area, but since the computation is equivalent to the standard Expected Calibration Error, we adopt the more common nomenclature used in the literature.

Regarding the Spearman correlation, we only report the results obtained with our method. Our approach achieves a relative improvement of 4.6% over ensemble-based correlation. We chose not to include this metric for all models because not every method provides a variance estimate, making a direct comparison, in our view, unfair.

Finally, using the calibration procedure described in the main paper and the NLL function in the appendix, we obtain cNLL = $33.28 \pm 4.40$, outperforming Deep Ensemble (cNLL = $95.95$). We note, however, that cNLL is inherently biased toward models trained with an NLL objective (e.g., GMM models achieve cNLL = 8.85). Consequently, while this metric can favor certain model classes, it is less informative for comparing fundamentally different approaches. In practical applications of MLIPs, point-wise prediction errors, calibration, and correlation metrics are more operationally relevant than NLL-based scores. For this reason, we focused on these metrics in the main comparison, though we are happy to include additional cNLL results for completeness in the appendix if desired.

We thank the reviewer for the prompt and constructive feedback.

**Regarding the ECE and Spearman correlation for the Ensemble model (Figure 20 of the Supplementary Material in Tan et al.)**, we would like to clarify the data split used in their analysis. As stated explicitly in the caption of Figure 20:

> “All ensembles are trained only on the initial training data of ammonia, and results shown above are tested on a testing set.”

This setup differs from the split used for the results reported in the main text of Tan et al. (and which we reproduced for consistency with their primary findings). Indeed, on page 2 of the supplementary material, Tan et al. further specify:

> “For the ammonia data set, first generation models were trained on 62 geometries and validated on 16 geometries to assess the models’ ability to bootstrap on few data points.”

To ensure a fair comparison with Figure 20, **we repeated our experiments using the full training dataset** (analogous to the “same data splits” configuration in their supplementary results). The small dataset and the few parameters of the model allow for very fast training (a couple of minutes) even with a single GPU. Unfortunately, we do not have access to the exact bagging indices required to reproduce the “different data splits” condition.

Our results under the same split as Figure 20 are:

- **MAE Energy (kcal/mol):** 11.44 ± 0.48  
- **MAE Forces (kcal/mol/Å):** 45.55 ± 1.69  
- **Spearman correlation:** 0.881 ± 0.024  
- **ECE:** 0.069 ± 0.004  

**Using this matching split, our method achieves lower MAE (energy and forces) and lower ECE than the Ensemble baseline**. For Spearman correlation, our model outperforms the “same hyperparameters, same data split” setting (the one used in our main paper), which reinforces our central results. While using different ensemble hyperparameters can increase the Spearman correlation by approximately 8% to ours, this comes at the cost of substantially higher MAE on both energy and forces, indicating that maintaining consistent hyperparameters (as done by Tan et al. in their main analysis) is more appropriate.

**Regarding the GMM (Gaussian Mixture Model) Spearman correlation reported in Figure 2 of Tan et al.**, as noted in our previous response, their analysis computes the Spearman correlation between **–NLL** and the **force error**, whereas we evaluate the correlation between **force variance** and **force error**. Since these target quantities are fundamentally different, the correlations are not directly comparable, and thus, we believe the comparison is not meaningful. **In order to compare with GMM, we have computed for BLIP the Spearman correlation between **–NLL** and the **force error**, and it is 0.944 ± 0.005, which outperforms 0.904 of what Tan et al report in Figure 2 of the main text**. 

We hope that this additional analysis further clarifies the reasoning behind our choices, and we sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive back-and-forth. Moreover, we hope that these clarifications help strengthen the contribution of our paper, and we would be grateful for any further feedback the reviewer may wish to share to improve the paper (for example add this analysis in the appendix if needed).

>Regarding (...) Figure 20 of the Supplementary Material in Tan et al.

Thank you for clearing this up. Your new results, training on the full n=78 training set fall nicely in line with the other results. Regarding the test/validation split, the only statement I found is: “We follow the same training/validation/test split protocol as Tan et al. (2023).” If I am not mistaken, I believe Tan et al use a single 80/20 split, and you use 4 random 80/20 splits? Or is it a single 80/20 split with 4 random initializations of the neural network?  Also, could you clarify exactly how the error bars are computed? It would be helpful to have this information clearly stated in the paper or supplementary material.

>Regarding the GMM (...) Spearman correlation (...) we believe the comparison is not meaningful.

I’m sorry, but I don’t quite follow this argument. Both the predicted variance and the -NLL of a GMM fitted to the final feature representation can be interpreted as measures of uncertainty. While they are different quantities—computed using different methods and on different scales—they both aim to capture how uncertain the model is about a prediction. The rank correlation metric evaluates how well these uncertainty measures correlate with the actual force error and is invariant under any nonlinear monotonic transformation. Therefore, it is meaningful to compare their rank correlations, even though the raw values themselves are not directly comparable.

>(...) we have computed for BLIP the Spearman correlation between –NLL and the force error (...)

Just to clarify, did you compute the correlation between the force error and the -NLL of the test data under your model? If so, this metric is problematic, as it effectively uses the test labels twice.

>the local reparameterization trick is not applicable (...) as it still requires sampling objects of similar complexity to the full weight matrix.

While this is not central to your contribution, I want to note that I believe it may be incorrect.

>(...) our method does perform amortized inference, but the amortization occurs over individual atomic structures rather than over an entire dataset.

Perhaps we may not reach agreement on this point. From my perspective, amortizing inference over atomic structures would imply having a posterior distribution for each atomic structure—that is, a model with latent variables defined per data point. As I understand your contribution, your model only has global parameters, so inference amortization on a per-input basis does not appear to be possible. In any case, I find the Bayesian interpretation somewhat unclear.

We thank the reviewer for their responsiveness and engagement throughout the rebuttal period. Your critical and constructive feedback has been extremely valuable in improving the paper. Below, we address the raised comments in light of our previous discussion.

> Thank you for clearing this up… It would be helpful to have this information clearly stated in the paper or supplementary material.

We thank the reviewer for the question. We use different network initialization seeds, which is already stated in each table caption (e.g., “Table 2: Expected calibration error for Forces in the Ammonia system for OOD data. **Averages are computed over 4 random initialization seeds**”). We would be happy to also include this information in the appendix if the reviewer believes it would add value to the paper.

>  I’m sorry, but I don’t quite follow this argument…. Just to clarify, did you compute the correlation…. 

Thank you for pointing this out! You are correct — we computed the correlation by passing the test data, which led to the confusion (we initially thought Tan et al. did the same!). We now agree that our model performs worse than the GMM on this specific metric, even though it still achieves better ECE and MAE. We appreciate you spotting this important detail and we added a column in Table 2 showing the Spearman correlation for clarity and fairness.

> Perhaps we may not reach agreement on this point….

We thank the reviewer for their feedback on amortization, which we found very helpful. While we use an inference network $E$ to predict structure-dependent uncertainty scale $\alpha(x)$, the variable $\theta$ remains global. In this sense, our method is partially amortized: the network $E$ amortizes the uncertainty across structures by reusing the same network to predict $\alpha$ for multiple structures, rather than optimizing $\alpha$ individually for each structure. On the other hand, the main latent variable $\theta$ is shared across all structures, distinguishing our approach from classical amortized inference. Consequently, the resulting posterior differs across structures only in the scale of its variance, which is amortized via the network $E$.

We would also like to emphasize that our method is Bayesian in spirit. The global latent variable $\theta$ is updated based on observed data (similarly to prior work on variational dropout [1,2]), and the posterior over the model weights reflects structure-dependent uncertainty, partially amortized through $\alpha(x)$. We are very open to hear more from the reviewer since we are interested in discussing more to improve the paper. 

[1] Kingma, Durk P., Tim Salimans, and Max Welling. "Variational dropout and the local reparameterization trick." Advances in neural information processing systems 28 (2015).

[2] Molchanov, Dmitry, Arsenii Ashukha, and Dmitry Vetrov. "Variational dropout sparsifies deep neural networks." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2017.

The paper introduces a Bayesian framework for learning potential energy surfaces (PESs) via equivariant message passing neural networks. Compared to the non-Bayesian setting, this approach in principle allows for uncertainty quantification. It is also claimed that predictive accuracy is improved through the Bayesian approach. 

In contrast to previous approaches which rely on (compute and memory intensive) ensemble methods, the presented method only introduced a light computational overhead for a given model. It is also flexible and can be incorporated into existing neural network potentials. 

This seems like a valuable contribution to the field.

strengths.value: The paper significantly contributes to an important problem and provides a novel approach to Bayesian modeling in computational chemistry.

weaknesses.value: The paper claims that the Bayesian approach improves predictive accuracy for out of distribution configurations, specifically out of equilibrium geometries. For out of equilibrium geometries (in case they have multireference character) even DFT will not provide accurate energies or forces, which makes this a quite fundamental issue. I have a difficult time believing that a Bayesian model should overcome this and would appreciate a more detailed elaboration, as well as an explanation of what precisely causes the gain in accuracy.

We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent evaluating our paper. We are very happy the reviewer finds that our method "significantly contributes to an important problem and provides a novel approach" based on Bayesian modelling. Below we address the few raised concerns in **weakness**:

> The paper claims that the Bayesian approach improves predictive accuracy for out of distribution...

In practice, for the ammonia experiment, we collected structures both near equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium. The model was trained only on near-equilibrium structures (with energies close to equilibrium) and then evaluated on structures with higher energies (out-of-equilibrium configurations). summary.value: The authors apply a variational Bayesian framework for machine learning interatomic potentials, used for molecular modeling and simulation. The goal of this framework is to better calibrate the model and quantify uncertainty when encountering new atomistic structures. The authors apply this method to training a model from scratch on ammonia data, and fine-tuning the Orbv3 model on a new dataset. The error is quantified based on the energy and force MAE.

strengths.value: - There is a need for MLIP uncertainty quantification methods, and the variational framework applied here has been less common for MLIPs.

weaknesses.value:
A number of my concerns around the paper are understanding what utility this approach has given the progress in the field. 

- The MLIP field now has models trained on large, broad datasets. The experiment of training a network from scratch feels unrealistic now, such as the first example the authors look at. They are also using an architecture (PaiNN) that is outdated, with many architectures having improved on this architecture. It’s not clear if this method can actually help the best models trained on large datasets, which is where the utility of the method would be.

- Error is only quantified by energy and force MAE, vs. other evaluation tasks. The BLIP error in Table 3 and Figure 3 is not very statistically significant to show that the method actually improves, even in the settings that the authors picked which don’t seem very relevant to where modern-day MLIPs are at now. The bar chart in Figure 3 is also highly misleading in the y-axis units.

- The models used and comparisons are also not the best ones. It is unclear if the method can actually make the best models better.

- This paper generally needs a lot of work, and it is very unclear if this method would actually be useful to use for MLIPs. This includes using the best models trained on a lot of data, more rigorously exploring out-of-distribution cases, and more rigorously quantifying the utility of the uncertainty estimates and performance improvements on downstream tasks. An example place to start would be models trained on the Open Molecules 2025 dataset.

questions.value:
- What does it look like if the method is used with an MLIP trained on larger datasets, such as eSEN or UMA? 

- Building on the above, can you show examples where the uncertainty quantification provided by this method is noticeably beneficial in some way?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent evaluating our paper. Below, we address the concerns raised in weakness.

#### Weaknesses:
> A number of my concerns around the paper are ...

We thank the reviewer for expressing the concern regarding the utility of our approach in the context of recent progress in the field. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to present a **scalable and efficient method** for prediction an uncertainty estimation in GNNs and MLIPs. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

1. *Extension of VAD to graph neural networks*: We generalize the VAD framework to GNNs, a contribution with broader relevance beyond MLIPs. We demonstrate that this approach is applicable for training GNNs (section 4.1) and, in particular, MLIPs (section 4.2 and 4.3).
2. *Applicability to both training-from-scratch and finetuning scenarios*: For MLIPs, our method offers two main advantages. **First, reduced training cost:** unlike ensemble-based approaches, our method trains only **one model**. In training-from-scratch settings, we match or exceed deterministic baselines, and ***at scale this could enable training a single model that achieves the same level of accuracy as standard MLIPs while additionally providing reliable uncertainty estimates at the same cost of compute and energy compared to standard MLIP approaches***. On the contrary ensembles need to train multiple model, and this is unfeasable for large scale trainings.
**Second, seamless finetuning of pretrained MLIPs:** unlike methods requiring multiple models or added uncertainty heads, our approach directly finetunes the existing pretrained weights and produces uncertainties using a single Universal MLIP (UMLIP). This is particularly valuable in realistic downstream tasks where only limited DFT data are available—allowing us to (1) adapt the model to the target system and (2) obtain meaningful uncertainty estimates for its predicted DFT energies. 


> The MLIP field now has models trained on large, broad datasets...

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We would like to clarify that our experiments **were not designed to be large-scale** due to computational constraints. To give a sense of scale, training the smallest UMA model (excluding hyperparameter optimization) requires roughly **10 days on 192 H200 140GB parallel GPUs** [1], which illustrates the high cost of large-scale MLIP training which **only few researchers have access to**.

The Ammonia experiment was chosen to **stress-test our method on heavily out-of-distribution (OOD) low data regime**. This experiment is taken from [2], which also reports the architecture and rationale behind the PaiNN choice (therefore we adapted on their setup). Importantly, we show that our model performs the best in terms of **accuracy** , and **calibration**, even when compared to strong baselines such as Deep Ensemble, which is considered to be SOTA in MLIP for UQ. We highlight that this test address realistic scenarios where some structures are naturally OOD for UMLIPs. In such cases, training from scratch is necessary to have a good surrogate. Given the high cost of DFT calculations, only a limited number of configurations are typically available (usually near equilibrium), making OOD conditions inevitable (in MD simulations for example). This is also noted in the paper, *“This is a common challenge in materials science, where training data may be biased toward equilibrium or near-equilibrium configurations.”*

> Error is only quantified by energy and force MAE...

We thank the reviewer for the comment. The Silica experiment was chosen because the dataset provides a **realistic and challenging benchmark**: the formation of large bulk structures makes DFT calculations expensive, and the structures are complex enough to be considered **out-of-distribution (OOD)** for universal MLIPs. Our results show that we can **effectively finetune a pretrained Universal MLIP (ORBv3 OMAT24) with BLIP**, achieving a **~7% improvement in force error** compared to standard MLIP finetuning and a **~10% improvement** compared to the pretrained network in the low-data regime. This is particularly important because generating labeled data is very costly. We also note that our method does **not degrade accuracy as data increases**, suggesting strong potential to generalize to larger datasets. Furthermore, our approach achieves a **substantial improvement in calibration** over Deep Ensemble Finetuning (0.032 vs. 0.247), showing that BLIP not only improves accuracy but also produces **more reliable uncertainty estimates**.

> The models used and comparisons are also not the best ones.... 

We thank the reviewer for the comment, we answer the point in the **Questions** section below, **we added a extra experiment to strengh the point**.

comment.value:
Below, we add the concerns raised in questions.

> What does it look like if the method is used with an MLIP trained on larger datasets, such as eSEN or UMA?

As noted in the paper, our method using the local reparameterization trick cannot currently be applied to architectures such as eSEN or UMA, which rely on learnable linear layers with irreducible representation dimensions. This does not mean that BLIP is incompatible with all equivariant architectures; rather, the local reparameterization trick (which enables scalability) can only be applied to certain architectures. We have added an in-depth discussion of this point and of equivariance in Appendix A (in blue), which open research directions for improvements. **Finally, we do apply our approach to ORBv3 trained on OMAT24, one of the most widely used universal MLIP datasets, and ORBv3 is considered among the state-of-the-art models.**

> Building on the above, can you show examples where the uncertainty quantification provided by this method is noticeably beneficial in some way?

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We have added an experiment using the very recent published MatPES [1] dataset (400K selected molecular structures) in an active learning loop for finetuing ORBv3, where uncertainties are used to improve the pretrained model by selecting the structures for which the model is most uncertain. After these structures are selected, reference DFT computations are performed, and the model is further fine-tuned. We repeat multiple time this cycle. The results show that BLIP with uncertainty-driven fine-tuning outperforms standard fine-tuning, in which molecules are selected at random, showing that uncertainties with BLIP can be used in an active learning loop. **The full results are reported in Section 4.4**

comment.value:
We thank you for your comments. We would like to clarify a few points regarding the scope and goal of our work, to better highlight its contributions and relevance. 

**Evaluation against relevant literature and SOTA models**:
Our experiments are designed to test our method against both relevant literature (e.g., Tan et al. [1]) and state-of-the-art models (e.g., Orbv3) in regimes where the base model is **not yet optimal**. This ensures that the observed improvements are meaningful for models that are limited either by architecture or data. In addition, to address the small-data regime specifically, we have included a new experiment using the MATEPES dataset (400K structures, section 4.4) to demonstrate applicability in different data scenarios.

**Clarification on Orbv3 experiments and metrics**:
We emphasize that our goal is not to find the best model in terms of absolute energy or force MAE or downstream tasks. Instead, **our focus is on introducing an efficient method for uncertainty quantification (UQ) while obtaining similar predictive performance**. While the Orbv3 direct force model was used for analysis, and energy/force MAE is reported, these metrics serve primarily as a benchmark rather than the end objective. *UQ in MLIPs is a rapidly growing field, and ensembling is currently the state-of-the-art approach; but it is computationally expensive (see Appendix E). We provide an efficient alternative that is competitive with ensembling and, in our experiments, demonstrates superior performance*.

**We stress that this is fundamentally a UQ paper, and our contribution lies in providing a scalable, efficient method for uncertainty quantification that can be applied across different models, including high-performing SOTA models**. The results highlight that our method is effective even when the underlying model is strong, opening new possibilities for UQ in molecular modelling applications.

 We sincerely appreciate your time, thoughtful feedback, and careful review and we remain open to discussion.

[1] Tan, Aik Rui, et al. "Single-model uncertainty quantification in neural network potentials does not consistently outperform model ensembles." npj Computational Materials 9.1 (2023): 225.

comment.value:
We are grateful to the reviewers for their insightful comments and constructive feedback. The rebuttal process facilitated meaningful discussions, and we have systematically addressed all technical issues highlighted. We provide below a summary of the main strengths recognised by the reviewers and the key concerns we have addressed through our revisions.

### Strengths highlighted by Reviewers

- **Novelty and relevance:** Reviewers **BtQJ, cqQ8, EYRq, and 3VJ2** agree that the paper tackles an important problem in *Uncertainty Quantification (UQ)* for *Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs)* and introduces a **novel variational framework** to address it.

- **Scalability:** Reviewer **cqQ8** highlights the **computational and memory scalability** of our method compared to existing, more resource-intensive UQ approaches.

- **General applicability:** Reviewers **cqQ8 and EYRq** note that our approach is not restricted to MLIPs; it is broadly applicable to **any Graph Neural Network**, extending its impact to a wide range of problems.

### Concerns addressed

1. **Small data regime and downstream task** (BtQJ, EYRq, 3VJ2)

The reviewers noted that most of our experiments were conducted in low-data regimes and that we did not demonstrate the use of uncertainties in a downstream task. We thank the reviewers for this observation and would like to clarify that our experiments were not designed to be large-scale due to computational constraints (e.g., training a universal MLIP such as UMA can require days on 200+ parallel H200 GPUs). Instead, we focused on **stress-testing our method under heavily out-of-distribution (OOD) and low-data conditions**, which is a common challenge in materials science where training data may be biased toward equilibrium structures or limited due to the high cost of DFT calculations.

**To further address this concern**, we have added a new experiment (Section 4.4) using the recently published MatPES dataset (*400K curated molecular structures*) in an **active learning loop** for fine-tuning ORBv3. In this setting, uncertainties are used to guide sample selection by choosing structures for which the model is most uncertain. The results show that **BLIP with uncertainty-driven fine-tuning outperforms standard fine-tuning**, where molecules are selected at random. This demonstrates that BLIP’s uncertainties can be effectively used in an active learning workflow.

***This new experiment satisfies both conditions identified by the reviewers: it operates in a large-data regime and incorporates uncertainties in a downstream task.***

2. **Literature review** (3VJ2, EYRq)

The reviewers noted that our related work section did not sufficiently cite prior uncertainty quantification methods for MLIPs. We thank the reviewers for this helpful suggestion, which allowed us to strengthen the paper. While the initial submission was constrained by the page limit, ***we have now added a dedicated paragraph addressing this point. The new text, together with additional references, is highlighted in blue in Section 2.4.***


3. **Computational efficiency analysis** (3VJ2, BtQJ)

The reviewers requested a more in-depth analysis of the computational efficiency of BLIP compared to state-of-the-art ensemble methods. **Accordingly, we have added a detailed discussion of parameter counts and FLOPs in Appendix E, including a direct comparison with Deep Ensembles.** The results show that BLIP’s parameter count remains roughly comparable to that of the underlying MLIP, whereas ensemble methods scale linearly with the number of models (i.e., an ensemble of size *N* requires *N*× parameters). Similarly, FLOPs for ensembles also grow linearly, while in BLIP we incur only a 2× increase in FLOPs during training and retain the **same FLOPs as the base MLIP for mean prediction**. 


4. **Equivariance analysis** (EYRq, cqQ8)

The reviewers noted that the equivariance properties of BLIP (and variational dropout) are an interesting contribution that deserves greater emphasis. In response, **we have added an Appendix section (Section A.3) where we formally prove that the BLIP update rule in Equation 7 preserves the equivariance of MLIP models**. We hope this clarification strengthens our argument and supports future readers in extending the methodology.


These revisions preserve the manuscript’s core contributions while adding the requested clarity and additional validation. We believe that all substantial concerns raised by the reviewers have been thoroughly addressed.

We hope this summary is helpful in the final evaluation of our work.

Best regards,  
The Authors

summary.value:
This paper proposes an architecture for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials that combines message passing neural networks with variational dropout. The authors motivate this architecture by its ability to quantify uncertainty, evaluating it in the low-data regime through out-of-distribution detection and active learning. There are several outstanding issues with the paper that make it unsuitable for publication in its current form. The major issues include:

* Utility of uncertainty quantification. In the original submission, the authors did not demonstrate the downstream utility of the uncertainty estimates provided by their proposed method. While they included a small active learning experiment in the revision, it is limited in scope and could benefit from further fleshing out.
* Model/training is (potentially) out-of-date. The MLIP field has generally converged on larger pretrained models that are fine-tuned for a downstream task. The authors claim their focus is on uncertainty quantification, not on achieving the “best” model. Nevertheless, if we consider the downstream use case of this uncertainty (selective classification, active learning, etc.), it is not clear whether this uncertainty would provide improved performance compared to using a modern state-of-the-art model. It is also possible that the community would not find such a model significant since it deviates from best practices.
* Comparison to other UQ methods. Although the authors included a discussion of Deep Ensembles after the rebuttal period, they did not provide a quantitative comparison. Even if, as the authors claim, deep ensembles may be computationally unrealistic, such a comparison would help to contextualize the performance of the proposed method.

reviewer_concerns.value: The reviewers who did not participate in post-rebuttal discussions raised concerns about the model being out of date. All other concerns involved a great deal of back-and-forth.

While I wish the reviewers had had the opportunity to engage more in discussion, I do not think their opinions would have changed. The authors would best address the concerns of relevance through experiments rather than debate, and so I think this paper would benefit from a major revision and another round of reviews.

- BtQJ responded to the authors’ rebuttal, and their mind wasn’t changed about whether the setup was out-of-date. I don’t think further discussion would have changed their mind.
- cqQ8 was positive, though the review was generally shallow and low confidence. If they had participated, I could imagine their score potentially decreasing based on the discussion from other reviewers.
- EYRq had a detailed conversation with the authors on the setup, additional results, and the Bayesian interpretation of their method. While some concerns were resolved, others seemed to be intractable points of disagreement (e.g. the Bayesian interpretation). It is possible that they would have increased their score given the chance.
- 3VJ2 did not participate during the discussion period at all, so my guess is that they probably would not have changed their score (or given a unsubstantiated score change that I likely would not have paid attention to).
